failure_modes.description: Queue length as primary determinant ignores intersection capacity constraints
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic engineering literature consistently shows that optimal timing requires balancing multiple factors including pedestrian crossing times, safety considerations, and intersection capacity, not just queue length.

failure_modes.description: Independent operation contradicts well-established traffic signal coordination principles
failure_modes.evidence: Decades of traffic engineering research demonstrate that coordinated signal systems (like bandwidth optimization or progressive signal systems) outperform isolated operation in nearly all urban scenarios.

failure_modes.description: Fails to account for overflow effects at intersection boundaries
failure_modes.evidence: Local adjustments would cause queue spillover to upstream intersections, creating cascading failures that the local controllers cannot detect or mitigate.

failure_modes.description: Local feedback control with coordination already exists in modern adaptive systems
failure_modes.evidence: Systems like SCATS and SCOOT already implement local feedback with coordination, making this approach neither novel nor superior to existing technology.

failure_modes.description: Expected oscillations would inevitably occur with competing local objectives
failure_modes.evidence: Game theory shows that when each intersection optimizes locally without considering network effects, Braess's paradox and similar phenomena create system-wide inefficiencies.

failure_modes.description: Slime mold analogy fundamentally misapplies biological principles to engineered systems
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems have non-negotiable physical constraints (vehicle dimensions, acceleration limits) and safety requirements that biological systems lack, making direct analogy invalid.
